0. Basic usage

Source: vignettes/ggexon-workflow.Rmd
ggexon-workflow.Rmd

From data to a genomic figure

Genomic figures often combine exon positions on a chromosome, links between genomes, signal depth, and positions along a protein. ggexon connects these views through stored annotations and a ggplot2 plotting grammar.

Each example below presents the input, constructs or prepares the ggexon object, and chooses geoms, scales, and a theme. The small gene models, gene-order matrix, protein counts, and DNA strings are synthetic teaching data. The pairwise, synteny, and coverage examples use bundled files. Run the chunks in order in an R session with the current version of ggexon installed.

library(ggexon)
library(ggplot2)

Major data objects

Object What it stores Typical input
SynFeatureAnnotation Genes, transcripts, exons, and CDS GFF3 or GTF
SynIndividual One genome or sample and its annotation layers Annotation, optional FASTA
SynSpecies Individuals and comparative relationships Individuals, alignments, homology, trees
SynPairAlignment, SynMultiAlignment Relationships between genomes PAF/PSL, or supported multiple-alignment data
SynBigWigAnnotation, SynVCFAnnotation Region-queryable signal or variants BigWig or VCF
SynProteinDomainAnnotation, SynProteinMutationAnnotation Domains or mutation summaries Domain and mutation tables
SynAnnotationPatch An explicit gene-model correction Corrected feature ranges
HomologyAnnotation Reference/query gene mappings Curated table or imported BLAST results
SynLayout, SynLocusSet Reusable panel windows or comparable loci Named coordinate windows

Plotting functions supplied by ggexon

ggexon() starts the figure. Syn-aware layers resolve stored annotations when the plot is built; table-based layers use prepared data. Ordinary ggplot2 scales and themes remain available. A theme changes appearance; it does not select a genomic window or transform coordinates.

Geoms

Function What it draws
geom_exon() Exon rectangles, transcript backbones, and strand direction
geom_exon2() Exon/CDS/UTR models with explicit introns and optional schematic compression
geom_genetag() One directional gene span, with optional labels and overlap lanes
geom_genebox() Equal-size gene boxes with internal strand arrows
geom_genelabel() Gene labels and their leader lines, including homology-based names
geom_genelink() Straight, elbow, or spline lines between supplied coordinate pairs
geom_nuclink() Nucleotide-alignment ribbons between genomic panels
geom_synteny_link() Interval ribbons for supplied gene, exon, or block relationships
geom_coverage() Continuous coverage or signal tracks
geom_motif() Motif/domain blocks; attached protein domains can be projected onto genomic CDS intervals
geom_aa_variant() Amino-acid variant markers projected onto transcript models
geom_protein_lollipop() A protein backbone, domain blocks, and mutation stems and heads
geom_mutation_label() Mutation labels positioned to match mutation markers
geom_alignseq() Anchored DNA-difference markers or aligned sequence rows
geom_genomic_tree() Attaches a rectangular tree for alignment with genomic panels

Scales and guides

Function What it controls
scale_x_ggexon_genomic() Shared exon-aware intron compression with original genomic coordinate labels
guide_x_ggexon_piecewise() Representative exon and intron scale bars for the compressed genomic x scale
strip_scale_x() Gene-order display widths or explicit shared comparison slots
strip_scale() Compatibility alias for strip_scale_x()
scale_x_facet_labels() Different x-axis labels for facets sharing a continuous x scale
scale_panel_annotation() Shared or independent annotation-panel y scales, with optional visible limits
scale_panel_coverage() Shared or independent coverage-panel y scales, with optional manual or automatic visible limits

Facets and panel layout

Function What it arranges
facet_genomics() Annotation, coverage, and intervening link panels
facet_genomictree() Genomic panels ordered by tree tips, beside one spanning tree
center_panel_annotation() Centers annotation bodies in their panel views
set_panel_xlim(), clear_panel_xlim() Store or clear per-individual genomic windows
effective_panel_windows() Inspect the annotation windows resolved for a plot or stored layout
locus_grid_layout(), use_locus_grid() Prepare and apply layouts for comparable locus windows
annotate_cross_panel() Connect explicitly supplied anchors across panels
link_panels() Connect matching IDs represented by anchors in different panels

Themes

Function When to use it
theme_ggexon_base() A background-free foundation retaining ordinary axes and grids
theme_ggexon_clean() The named shortcut for that clean background-free styling
theme_ggexon_track() Compact genomic tracks, with control over axes, grids, and legends
theme_ggexon_pairwise() Stacked annotation/link/annotation comparisons
theme_ggexon_genomictree() Genomic tracks aligned beside a tree
theme_ggexon_side_strips() Horizontal facet labels on the left or right, added after a complete theme

Plot preparation and output

Function What it prepares
alignseq_data() Anchored columns and difference events from two already aligned DNA strings
protein_lollipop_data() Protein backbone, domain, and mutation layout tables
protein_mutation_data() Access the normalized table in a protein-mutation annotation
syn_gr_to_exon_df() Convert genomic feature ranges to an exon plotting table
project_domains_to_genome(), project_mutations_to_genome() Map protein positions through transcript CDS blocks to genomic intervals
ggexon_output_size() Record the intended figure dimensions for downstream layout

Functions such as aes(), scale_fill_manual(), scale_x_continuous(), facet_wrap(), coord_fixed(), theme(), and ggsave() come from ggplot2. The examples combine these with the ggexon functions above.

Curating elements within data objects

Curation verbs describe the change made to stored biological information. Updating selected fields differs from replacing a complete gene model; resetting patches restores the base annotation.

Operation Function Effect
Add relationships add_homology() Insert query-to-reference gene relationships
Update fields update_homology() Change supplied columns for matched query genes while preserving other fields
Remove relationships remove_homology() Remove selected homology rows, with an optional reference-gene guard
Set display labels set_gene_labels() Assign labels while retaining stable biological IDs
Map identifiers map_domain_ids() Map domain annotation identifier values to the key used by transcript models
Patch gene models patch_annotation() Record an addition, replacement, or removal using mode = "add", "replace", or "remove"
Reset patches reset_patches() Restore the base feature annotation and retain assigned display labels

replace_homology(), delete_homology(), rename_domain_annotation_ids(), and clear_patches() remain supported aliases for the corresponding operations above. Patch mode "drop" remains an alias for "remove". Use query_*() to inspect data and subset_*() or filter_*() to select the data to keep.

1. Exons and alternative transcripts

An exon table contains intervals and transcript membership. Drawing each row as an unrelated rectangle loses introns and strand direction. geom_exon() uses the feature hierarchy to draw transcript models.

Present the input

Create two synthetic genes on chr1. Gene A has a full transcript and an exon-skipping transcript; gene B is on the opposite strand. Coordinates are one-based and inclusive, as in GTF. These are teaching models, not observed gene annotations.

features <- data.frame(
  type = c("gene", "transcript", rep("exon", 3), rep("CDS", 3),
           "transcript", rep("exon", 2), rep("CDS", 2),
           "gene", "transcript", "exon", "exon"),
  start = c(101, 101, 101, 501, 901, 101, 501, 901,
            101, 101, 901, 101, 901, 1201, 1201, 1201, 1501),
  end = c(960, 960, 160, 590, 960, 160, 590, 960,
          960, 160, 960, 160, 960, 1560, 1560, 1260, 1560),
  strand = c(rep("+", 13), rep("-", 4)),
  gene_id = c(rep("geneA", 13), rep("geneB", 4)),
  transcript_id = c(NA, rep("A_full", 7), rep("A_skip", 5),
                    NA, rep("B_only", 3))
)
knitr::kable(features)
type start end strand gene_id transcript_id
gene 101 960 + geneA NA
transcript 101 960 + geneA A_full
exon 101 160 + geneA A_full
exon 501 590 + geneA A_full
exon 901 960 + geneA A_full
CDS 101 160 + geneA A_full
CDS 501 590 + geneA A_full
CDS 901 960 + geneA A_full
transcript 101 960 + geneA A_skip
exon 101 160 + geneA A_skip
exon 901 960 + geneA A_skip
CDS 101 160 + geneA A_skip
CDS 901 960 + geneA A_skip
gene 1201 1560 - geneB NA
transcript 1201 1560 - geneB B_only
exon 1201 1260 - geneB B_only
exon 1501 1560 - geneB B_only

Write the records as a standard nine-column GTF. Substitute your own GTF or GFF3 path when working with real annotations.

attributes <- paste0('gene_id "', features$gene_id, '";')
has_transcript <- !is.na(features$transcript_id)
attributes[has_transcript] <- paste0(
  attributes[has_transcript], ' transcript_id "',
  features$transcript_id[has_transcript], '";'
)
gtf <- data.frame(
  seqname = "chr1", source = "synthetic", type = features$type,
  start = features$start, end = features$end, score = ".",
  strand = features$strand,
  phase = ifelse(features$type == "CDS", "0", "."), attributes = attributes
)
gtf_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".gtf")
write.table(gtf, gtf_file, sep = "\t", quote = FALSE,
            row.names = FALSE, col.names = FALSE)

Construct and inspect the object

SynIndividual(annotation_file = ...) attaches a default SynFeatureAnnotation. A FASTA is optional for annotation plotting; sequence extraction and translation require one. load_annotation() materializes the features so that we can inspect them before drawing.

model <- SynIndividual(
  annotation_file = gtf_file, annotation_format = "gtf", id = "teaching"
)
model <- load_annotation(model)
class(model)
#> [1] "SynIndividual"
#> attr(,"package")
#> [1] "ggexon"
class(get_annotation(model))
#> [1] "SynFeatureAnnotation"
#> attr(,"package")
#> [1] "ggexon"
exons <- query_features(model, feature_type = "exon", all = TRUE)
knitr::kable(as.data.frame(exons)[,
  c("seqnames", "start", "end", "strand", "gene_id", "transcript_id")])
seqnames start end strand gene_id transcript_id
chr1 101 160 + geneA A_full
chr1 501 590 + geneA A_full
chr1 901 960 + geneA A_full
chr1 101 160 + geneA A_skip
chr1 901 960 + geneA A_skip
chr1 1201 1260 - geneB B_only
chr1 1501 1560 - geneB B_only

Choose the geom, scales, and theme

Map transcript IDs to fill to distinguish isoforms. The ordinary continuous x scale preserves genomic spacing. The track theme hides the y axis used to position models; show_legend = TRUE retains the transcript legend. Use transcript_arrow_length = 30 for a fixed 30-bp horizontal triangle width on every transcript. transcript_arrow_ratio controls the triangle’s height relative to exon height, rather than its length along the x axis.

transcript_colours <- c(A_full = "#0072B2", A_skip = "#D55E00", B_only = "#009E73")
p_exons <- ggexon(model) +
  geom_exon(
    aes(fill = transcript_id), chr = "chr1", subset = c(80, 1600),
    transcript_arrow_length = 30
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = transcript_colours, name = "Transcript") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(100, 500, 900, 1300, 1600),
                     labels = scales::label_number(big.mark = ",")) +
  theme_ggexon_track(base_size = 10, show_legend = TRUE)
p_exons

The x distances are base pairs. The missing middle exon in A_skip comes from the input annotation; ggexon does not infer alternative splicing.

Compare the same annotation with other geoms

The same model can support several views. Keep chromosome 1 and the same genomic window, then choose a geom according to the detail you want to show.

geom_exon2(): exon and intron structure

geom_exon2() keeps the three transcript rows and draws introns as chevrons between exon blocks. Reuse the transcript colours from p_exons. compress_introns = FALSE preserves genomic distances for this comparison; the next example shows its schematic compression option.

p_exon2 <- ggexon(model) +
  geom_exon2(
    aes(fill = transcript_id), chr = "chr1", subset = c(80, 1600),
    compress_introns = FALSE, arrow_width = 12
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = transcript_colours, name = "Transcript") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(80, 1600),
                     breaks = c(100, 500, 900, 1300, 1600),
                     labels = scales::label_number(big.mark = ",")) +
  theme_ggexon_track(base_size = 10, show_legend = TRUE)
p_exon2

A compact transcript schematic

Long introns can dominate a transcript diagram and make exon structure hard to see. Use compress_introns = TRUE when you want a compact cartoon of exon order and exon skipping. Exon widths are retained, while intron_width = 50 replaces each intron with a 50-unit schematic gap.

p_exon2_schematic <- ggexon(model) +
  geom_exon2(
    aes(fill = transcript_id), chr = "chr1", subset = c(80, 1600),
    compress_introns = TRUE, intron_width = 50, arrow_width = 12
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = transcript_colours, name = "Transcript") +
  theme_ggexon_track(
    base_size = 10, show_legend = TRUE,
    show_x_axis = FALSE, show_x_grid = FALSE
  )
p_exon2_schematic

Each transcript is rearranged independently, so shared exons may no longer line up across isoforms. Hide the x axis and grid because these schematic positions do not represent shared genomic coordinates. The next section uses scale_x_ggexon_genomic() to compress introns while keeping transcripts and other genomic layers aligned.

geom_genetag(): whole-gene spans

geom_genetag() draws one directional span per gene. Gene A’s two isoforms therefore become one gene-level shape, and individual exons are no longer shown. Map fill to gene_id and use a gene palette for the two genes. Set arrow_width = 50 to give both strand-direction triangles the same 50-bp width, independent of gene length. Set ylim in coord_cartesian() to leave vertical space around the tags.

gene_colours <- c(geneA = "#0072B2", geneB = "#009E73")
p_gene_spans <- ggexon(model) +
  geom_genetag(
    aes(fill = gene_id), chr = "chr1", subset = c(80, 1600),
    show_label = FALSE, arrow_width = 50
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = gene_colours, name = "Gene") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(80, 1600),
                     breaks = c(100, 500, 900, 1300, 1600),
                     labels = scales::label_number(big.mark = ",")) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-1, 2)) +
  theme_ggexon_track(base_size = 10, show_legend = TRUE)
p_gene_spans

geom_genebox(): gene positions and strand

geom_genebox() draws equal-size squares with internal strand arrows. Query the same model’s gene rows and place each square at the midpoint of its annotated span. Using this table includes both genes, including gene B, which has no CDS records in the teaching annotation.

Here box_size = 120 sets a fixed display size, and coord_fixed(ratio = 1) keeps the boxes square. Their positions remain genomic coordinates; their widths do not represent gene lengths. The hidden y axis only positions the boxes.

gene_rows <- as.data.frame(query_features(
  model, chr = "chr1", start = 80, end = 1600, feature_type = "gene"
))
gene_rows$x <- (gene_rows$start + gene_rows$end) / 2
gene_rows$y <- 0

p_gene_boxes <- ggexon(gene_rows) +
  geom_genebox(aes(x = x, y = y, strand = strand, fill = gene_id),
               box_size = 120) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = gene_colours, name = "Gene") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(80, 1600),
                     breaks = c(100, 500, 900, 1300, 1600),
                     labels = scales::label_number(big.mark = ",")) +
  coord_fixed(ratio = 1, ylim = c(-120, 120)) +
  theme_ggexon_track(base_size = 10, show_legend = TRUE)
p_gene_boxes

2. Compress introns while retaining genomic labels

Long introns can make exons too small to compare. A shared exon-aware scale compresses gaps while keeping transcripts aligned, helping you compare exon structure across isoforms.

Present the input

Reuse the synthetic GTF and inspect gene A’s exon rows.

knitr::kable(features[features$gene_id == "geneA" & features$type == "exon", ])
type start end strand gene_id transcript_id
3 exon 101 160 + geneA A_full
4 exon 501 590 + geneA A_full
5 exon 901 960 + geneA A_full
10 exon 101 160 + geneA A_skip
11 exon 901 960 + geneA A_skip

Prepare the object

Create a copy restricted to the first locus, leaving model reusable.

gene_a <- subset_individual(model, chr = "chr1", start = 80, end = 980)
query_features(gene_a, feature_type = "exon", all = TRUE)
#> GRanges object with 5 ranges and 7 metadata columns:
#>       seqnames    ranges strand |    source        type     score       phase
#>          <Rle> <IRanges>  <Rle> |  <factor> <character> <numeric> <character>
#>   [1]     chr1   101-160      + | synthetic        exon        NA        <NA>
#>   [2]     chr1   501-590      + | synthetic        exon        NA        <NA>
#>   [3]     chr1   901-960      + | synthetic        exon        NA        <NA>
#>   [4]     chr1   101-160      + | synthetic        exon        NA        <NA>
#>   [5]     chr1   901-960      + | synthetic        exon        NA        <NA>
#>           gene_id transcript_id   gene_name
#>       <character>   <character> <character>
#>   [1]       geneA        A_full       geneA
#>   [2]       geneA        A_full       geneA
#>   [3]       geneA        A_full       geneA
#>   [4]       geneA        A_skip       geneA
#>   [5]       geneA        A_skip       geneA
#>   -------
#>   seqinfo: 1 sequence from an unspecified genome; no seqlengths

Choose the geom, scales, and theme

geom_exon2() draws explicit chevron introns. scale_x_ggexon_genomic() applies a shared transformation to the original genomic coordinates, taking precedence over the geom’s schematic compression. A factor of 8 displays eligible gaps at one eighth of their genomic length while preserving exon widths.

p_compressed <- ggexon(gene_a) +
  geom_exon2(
    aes(fill = transcript_id), chr = "chr1", compress_introns = FALSE,
    arrow_width = 12
  ) +
  scale_x_ggexon_genomic(intron_factor = 8, n.breaks = 4) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = transcript_colours, name = "Transcript") +
  theme_ggexon_track(base_size = 10, show_legend = TRUE)
p_compressed

Ticks report original genomic positions, but equal display distances across exons and introns no longer imply equal base-pair distances. A piecewise guide can show separate representative exon and intron scale bars. The solid exon bar and dashed intron bar share one horizontal baseline; labels show their original lengths in bp. Use linewidth to set the thickness of both bars and their end ticks in millimetres.

ggexon(gene_a) +
  geom_exon2(
    aes(fill = transcript_id), chr = "chr1", compress_introns = FALSE,
    arrow_width = 12
  ) +
  scale_x_ggexon_genomic(
    intron_factor = 8,
    guide = guide_x_ggexon_piecewise(by = "panel", linewidth = 0.6)
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = transcript_colours) +
  theme_ggexon_track(base_size = 10)

With explicit CDS and UTR records, geom_exon2(annotation_type = "all") can distinguish their box heights.

3. Gene spans and readable labels

For a locus overview, transcript detail can hide gene order. A directional tag gives one span per gene. Separate labels keep names readable without replacing the stable gene IDs used in computation.

Present the input 

knitr::kable(features[features$type == "gene",
                      c("gene_id", "start", "end", "strand")])
gene_id start end strand
1 geneA 101 960 +
14 geneB 1201 1560 - 
labels <- c(geneA = "Gene A (two isoforms)", geneB = "Gene B")

Prepare the object

set_gene_labels() returns an updated object carrying plot labels alongside the original IDs.

labelled_model <- set_gene_labels(model, labels)

Choose the geom, scales, and theme

Suppress built-in tag labels and add geom_genelabel() for explicit placement. collapse_tandem = TRUE also combines adjacent genes sharing a label. Use the same x limits, c(80, 1600), and y limits, c(-1, 2), as in p_gene_spans to keep the gene bodies near the middle of the plot. Set fontface = "italic" in geom_genelabel() to italicize the displayed gene names.

p_gene_labels <- ggexon(labelled_model) +
  geom_genetag(
    aes(fill = gene_id), chr = "chr1", subset = c(80, 1600),
    show_label = FALSE, arrow_width = 50
  ) +
  geom_genelabel(
    chr = "chr1", subset = c(80, 1600), label_direction = "top",
    size = 3, fontface = "italic", collapse_tandem = TRUE,
    panel_width_inch = 7
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = gene_colours) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(80, 1600),
                     breaks = c(100, 500, 900, 1300, 1600),
                     labels = scales::label_number(big.mark = ",")) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-1, 2)) +
  theme_ggexon_track(base_size = 10)
p_gene_labels

For crowded loci, gene_layout = "stack" or "nested" separates overlapping bodies. For cross-species names, attach a HomologyAnnotation to a SynSpecies and use it through geom_genelabel(). Labels alone do not establish homology.

4. Pairwise nucleotide alignments

Two genomes can contain the same locus at different chromosome positions. SynSpecies stores their annotations and alignment together; facet_genomics() places links between their source tracks.

Present the input

Use the bundled XZ1516 and N2 annotations and a small PAF alignment. This example needs neither a download nor user-supplied files.

compact_dir <- system.file("extdata", "compact_synspecies", package = "ggexon")
xz_gff <- file.path(compact_dir, "caenorhabditis_XZ1516.gff3")
n2_gtf <- file.path(compact_dir, "c_elegans.PRJNA13758.WS285.canonical_geneset.gtf")
paf_file <- file.path(compact_dir, "V_alginment.paf")
stopifnot(file.exists(xz_gff), file.exists(n2_gtf), file.exists(paf_file))
cat(readLines(xz_gff, n = 5), sep = "\n")
#> ##gff-version 3
#> III_RagTag   funannotate gene    448 2094    .   -   .   ID=FUN_000001;
#> III_RagTag   funannotate mRNA    448 2094    .   -   .   ID=FUN_000001-T1;Parent=FUN_000001;product=hypothetical protein;
#> III_RagTag   funannotate exon    1994    2094    .   -   .   ID=FUN_000001-T1.exon1;Parent=FUN_000001-T1;
#> III_RagTag   funannotate exon    735 1344    .   -   .   ID=FUN_000001-T1.exon2;Parent=FUN_000001-T1;
cat(readLines(n2_gtf, n = 3), sep = "\n")
#> V    WormBase    gene    20448270    20453184    .   -   .   gene_id "WBGene00009848"; gene_version "1"; gene_source "WormBase"; gene_biotype "protein_coding"; gene_name "F48F5.6";
#> V    WormBase    transcript  20448275    20449959    .   -   .   gene_id "WBGene00009848"; gene_version "1"; transcript_id "F48F5.6a.1"; gene_source "WormBase"; gene_biotype "protein_coding"; transcript_source "WormBase"; transcript_biotype "protein_coding";
#> V    WormBase    exon    20449750    20449959    .   -   .   gene_id "WBGene00009848"; gene_version "1"; transcript_id "F48F5.6a.1"; exon_number "1"; gene_source "WormBase"; gene_biotype "protein_coding"; transcript_source "WormBase"; transcript_biotype "protein_coding"; exon_id "F48F5.6a.1.e1";
raw_paf <- read.delim(paf_file, header = FALSE, comment.char = "")
names(raw_paf)[1:12] <- c(
  "query", "qlen", "qstart", "qend", "strand", "target", "tlen",
  "tstart", "tend", "matches", "alen", "mapq"
)
knitr::kable(head(raw_paf[, c("query", "qstart", "qend", "strand", "alen")], 4))
query qstart qend strand alen
V_RagTag 21580812 21581913 + 1104
V_RagTag 21581910 21584356 - 2552
V_RagTag 21579732 21580830 - 1131
V_RagTag 21574445 21579192 - 5159 
knitr::kable(head(raw_paf[, c("target", "tstart", "tend", "matches", "mapq")], 4))
target tstart tend matches mapq
V 18218473 18219520 793 255
V 20456948 20459445 2225 255
V 20459441 20460565 1025 255
V 20460561 20465040 3806 255

Raw PAF uses zero-based starts and half-open intervals. The ggexon importer normalizes returned start/end columns to one-based closed intervals. Let it perform this conversion once.

Construct and inspect the objects 

xz <- SynIndividual(annotation_file = xz_gff, id = "XZ1516")
n2 <- SynIndividual(annotation_file = n2_gtf, annotation_format = "gtf", id = "N2")
comparison <- SynSpecies(name = "Caenorhabditis pair")
comparison <- add_individual(comparison, xz)
comparison <- add_individual(comparison, n2)
comparison <- add_pairwise_alignment(
  comparison,
  SynPairAlignment(
    name = "XZ1516_vs_N2", query_individual = "XZ1516",
    target_individual = "N2", file = paf_file, format = "paf"
  )
)
individual_names(comparison)
#> [1] "XZ1516" "N2"
aligned_blocks <- pairwise_alignment_data(
  comparison, alignment = "XZ1516_vs_N2",
  subset = c(XZ1516 = "RagTag_V:21574445-21584356"), filter = 200
)
knitr::kable(head(aligned_blocks[, intersect(
  c("qname", "qstart", "qend", "tname", "tstart", "tend", "strand", "alen"),
  names(aligned_blocks)
)], 6))
qstart qend tstart tend strand alen
21580813 21581913 18218474 18219520 + 1104
21581911 21584356 20456949 20459445 - 2552
21579733 21580830 20459442 20460565 - 1131
21574446 21579192 20460562 20465040 - 5159

filter = 200 removes short alignment fragments from this query result, leaving the stored alignment unchanged. subset_pairwise_alignment() and filter_pairwise_alignment() expose these operations separately.

Choose the geom, scales, facet, and theme

geom_nuclink() derives a comparison window from XZ1516 coordinates and resolves the corresponding N2 region. Independent x ranges show each genome’s own positions. The annotation y policy controls model layout. Hide the link panel’s axes because the ribbons connect the two annotation rulers rather than defining a third genomic coordinate system.

p_pairwise <- ggexon(comparison) +
  geom_exon(species = c("N2", "XZ1516"), fill = "#0072B2") +
  geom_nuclink(
    reference = "XZ1516", chr = "RagTag_V",
    subset = c(21574445, 21584356), alignment = "XZ1516_vs_N2",
    fill = "#56B4E9", alpha = 0.55
  ) +
  facet_genomics(vars(track), scales = "free_x", ncol = 1,
                 strip.position = "left", vertical = "center",
                 link_axis = "none", link_strip = "blank", link_panel_height = 0.6) +
  scale_panel_annotation("fixed_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_number(big.mark = ",")) +
  theme_ggexon_pairwise(base_size = 10)
p_pairwise

The GFF uses V_RagTag; the resolver also accepts the RagTag_V alias used in the plotting call. Inspect seqnames when preparing your own files.

Omitting species on a SynSpecies exon layer selects all stored individuals. Select it explicitly for a subset. For repeated figures, set_panel_xlim() stores named per-individual windows on the comparison’s SynLayout; clear_panel_xlim() removes the overrides.

SynMultiAlignment supports ODGI-backed comparisons. It can store already parsed MAF data through data, but load_alignment() does not parse MAF files. See the alignment class reference for supported inputs.

5. Local synteny from real alignment blocks

Reuse the comparison object from the previous example. Gene tags show the annotated gene spans, and geom_synteny_link() connects the stored PAF alignment intervals. Both layers read from the same SynSpecies object.

Present the input

The comparison object already contains the XZ1516 GFF3, N2 WS285 GTF, and XZ1516_vs_N2 alignment. Select a local window in each assembly using its chromosome name: V_RagTag for XZ1516 and V for N2.

Set the windows on the object

store_chain_layout() creates the annotation-link-annotation panel layout. set_panel_xlim() then stores each assembly’s window on that layout. The geoms use these windows to select gene annotations and alignment blocks when the plot is built.

local_synteny <- store_chain_layout(
  comparison, free = list(x = TRUE, y = FALSE)
)
local_synteny <- set_panel_xlim(
  local_synteny, individual = c("XZ1516", "N2"),
  xlim = list(XZ1516 = c(21574000, 21585000), N2 = c(20456500, 20465500)),
  xlim_chr = c(XZ1516 = "V_RagTag", N2 = "V")
)
effective_panel_windows(local_synteny)
#>   PANEL  track panel_type individual      chr    start      end
#> 1     1 XZ1516 annotation     XZ1516 V_RagTag 21574000 21585000
#> 3     3     N2 annotation         N2        V 20456500 20465500

Two N2 genes and four XZ1516 genes lie in these windows. Three alignment blocks remain, all in reverse orientation. The fourth PAF hit maps outside the selected N2 locus and is excluded by the panel windows. This creates a new object carrying the local layout; comparison remains available for other views.

Choose the geom, scales, facet, and theme

Pass local_synteny directly to ggexon(). Use grey tags for the genes and one blue fill for all alignment ribbons. gene_layout = "stack" separates the overlapping N2 gene spans. Built-in tag labels use the annotation names, with label_fontface = "italic" and label_position = "outside" to place them above the gene bodies. Independent base-pair axes retain each assembly’s coordinates; the middle panel has no genomic axis of its own.

p_synteny <- ggexon(local_synteny) +
  geom_genetag(
    fill = "grey75", colour = "grey35", arrow_width = 100,
    gene_layout = "stack", label_size = 2.5,
    label_fontface = "italic", label_position = "outside"
  ) +
  geom_synteny_link(
    alignment = "XZ1516_vs_N2", fill = "#56B4E9", alpha = 0.5
  ) +
  facet_genomics(vars(track), scales = "free_x", ncol = 1,
                 strip.position = "left", vertical = "center",
                 link_axis = "none", link_strip = "blank", link_panel_height = 0.6) +
  scale_panel_annotation("fixed_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_number(big.mark = ",")) +
  theme_ggexon_pairwise(base_size = 10)
p_synteny

The ribbons show sequence-alignment spans, not independently curated gene-to-gene orthology assignments. A ribbon may cross several gene tags. geom_synteny_link() resolves the alignment stored in local_synteny without inferring gene relationships. Neither layer needs a separately prepared plotting table.

6. RNA-seq coverage beside gene annotation

RNA-seq coverage and gene models share genomic coordinates but use different y scales. Here forward- and reverse-strand testis RNA-seq from D. sechellia occupy separate panels above the two gene models, CG42797 and Ptpmeg2. Both signal annotations and the gene models belong to one individual in a SynSpecies object.

Present the input

Reuse the bundled GTF and forward- and reverse-strand BigWigs from the local synteny tutorial. These files use chromosome-X coordinates on the D. sechellia assembly GCF_004382195.1. Keep the full tutorial window, with a one-base display margin, to include both genes. The GTF contains CDS and UTR pieces for the two mapped transcript models. The BigWig backend runs on macOS and Linux, and is unsupported on Windows.

rna_dir <- system.file("extdata", "dox_synteny", "objects", package = "ggexon")
rna_gtf <- file.path(rna_dir, "Dsech.gtf")
rna_plus_file <- file.path(rna_dir, "Dsech.RNAplus.bw")
rna_minus_file <- file.path(rna_dir, "Dsech.RNAminus.bw")
rna_window <- c(9396968L, 9444822L)
cat(readLines(rna_gtf, n = 8), sep = "\n")
#> ##gff-version 2
#> ##source-version rtracklayer 1.66.0
#> ##date 2026-10-27
#> X    ggexon_curated_Dox_demo UTR 9396969 9397323 .   +   .   gene_id "Dsech_CG42797"; gene_name "CG42797"; transcript_id "Dsech_NM_132346.3"
#> X    ggexon_curated_Dox_demo gene    9396969 9410256 .   +   .   gene_id "Dsech_CG42797"; gene_name "CG42797";
#> X    ggexon_curated_Dox_demo transcript  9396969 9410256 .   +   .   gene_id "Dsech_CG42797"; gene_name "CG42797"; transcript_id "Dsech_NM_132346.3"
#> X    ggexon_curated_Dox_demo CDS 9397324 9397422 .   +   .   gene_id "Dsech_CG42797"; gene_name "CG42797"; transcript_id "Dsech_NM_132346.3"
#> X    ggexon_curated_Dox_demo CDS 9397483 9397637 .   +   .   gene_id "Dsech_CG42797"; gene_name "CG42797"; transcript_id "Dsech_NM_132346.3"

The two BigWigs retain the deposited RNA-seq signal scores from testis biological replicate 1. They are not raw read counts. RNA_plus represents the forward transcript strand; RNA_minus stores the reverse-strand scores as positive values. CG42797 is on the plus strand and Ptpmeg2 is on the minus strand.

Construct and inspect the objects 

rna_individual <- SynIndividual(
  id = "Dsech", annotation_file = rna_gtf, annotation_format = "gtf",
  metadata = list(assembly = "GCF_004382195.1")
)
rna_individual <- add_annotation(rna_individual, SynBigWigAnnotation(
  name = "RNA_plus", bigwig_file = rna_plus_file,
  metadata = list(transcript_strand = "+", signal_unit = "deposited signal")
))
rna_individual <- add_annotation(rna_individual, SynBigWigAnnotation(
  name = "RNA_minus", bigwig_file = rna_minus_file,
  metadata = list(transcript_strand = "-", signal_unit = "deposited signal",
                  score_handling = "positive reverse-strand scores")
))
rna_comparison <- add_individual(
  SynSpecies(name = "D. sechellia testis RNASeq"), rna_individual
)
individual_names(rna_comparison)
#> [1] "Dsech"

head(as.data.frame(query_signal(
  get_annotation(rna_individual, "RNA_minus"), chr = "X",
  start = rna_window[1], end = rna_window[2]
)))
#>   seqnames   start     end width strand score
#> 1        X 9398376 9398376     1      *  0.99
#> 2        X 9398377 9398377     1      *  0.99
#> 3        X 9398378 9398378     1      *  0.99
#> 4        X 9398379 9398379     1      *  0.99
#> 5        X 9398380 9398380     1      *  0.99
#> 6        X 9398381 9398381     1      *  0.99

query_signal() inspects the stored signal as intervals with a score. The returned coordinates are 1-based inclusive. This inspection is separate from plotting: each geom below reads directly from rna_comparison.

Give each strand its own panel

Store a three-row layout on the object. track names the panels; the individual and species columns connect each row to the stored D. sechellia individual. RNASeq + and RNASeq - are two coverage-panel aliases for that same individual. The gene annotation occupies the third panel, with the Dsech ID. All three rows share the same genomic window.

species_layout(rna_comparison) <- SynLayout(
  panels = data.frame(
    PANEL = 1:3, ROW = 1:3, COL = 1L,
    track = c("RNASeq +", "RNASeq -", "Dsech"),
    panel_type = c("coverage", "coverage", "annotation"),
    individual = c("Dsech", "Dsech", NA_character_),
    species = c(NA_character_, NA_character_, "Dsech"),
    xlim_chr = "X", xlim_min = rna_window[1], xlim_max = rna_window[2]
  ),
  free = list(x = FALSE, y = TRUE)
)

Choose the geom, scales, facet, and theme

Select a panel alias with species in each geom_coverage() layer and choose its stored BigWig with annotation. This routes the forward signal to RNASeq + and the reverse signal to RNASeq -, while both layers read from the same individual. scale_panel_coverage("free_y") gives each panel its own y-range and axis. Both signals retain their original scores.

rna_gene_colours <- c(CG42797 = "#0072B2", Ptpmeg2 = "#009E73")

geom_exon2(annotation_type = "all") draws thick CDS and thinner UTR pieces, with genomic intron lengths retained. Both annotation layers explicitly select Dsech. Gene models and coverage share an uncompressed genomic x-axis.

coverage_plot <- ggexon(rna_comparison) +
  geom_coverage(
    species = "RNASeq +", annotation = "RNA_plus", fill = "#0072B2", alpha = 0.8
  ) +
  geom_coverage(
    species = "RNASeq -", annotation = "RNA_minus", fill = "#009E73", alpha = 0.8
  ) +
  geom_exon2(
    aes(ymin = 1, fill = gene_name, colour = gene_name),
    species = "Dsech", chr = "X", subset = rna_window, annotation_type = "all",
    exon_height = 0.45, cds_height = 1, utr_height = 0.45,
    compress_introns = FALSE, arrow_width = 450, linewidth = 0.2,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_genelabel(
    aes(ymin = 1, colour = gene_name), species = "Dsech", chr = "X",
    subset = rna_window, exon_height = 0.45, label_direction = "bottom",
    label_offset_fraction = 0.12,
    fontface = "italic", size = 3, show_link = FALSE, show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  facet_genomics(vars(track), ncol = 1, strip.position = "left",
                 coverage_panel_height = 1 / 3,
                 labeller = as_labeller(c("RNASeq +" = "RNASeq +",
                                          "RNASeq -" = "RNASeq -",
                                          Dsech = "D. sechellia"))) +
  scale_panel_annotation("free_y", limits = list(Dsech = c(0.84, 1.48))) +
  scale_panel_coverage("free_y") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = rna_gene_colours, guide = "none") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = rna_gene_colours, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = rna_window,
                     breaks = seq(9400000, 9440000, by = 10000),
                     labels = scales::label_number(scale = 1e-6, suffix = " Mb",
                                                    accuracy = 0.01),
                     oob = scales::oob_keep) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    name = "RNASeq signal", breaks = seq(0, 150, by = 25),
    guide = guide_axis(check.overlap = TRUE),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.08))
  ) +
  labs(x = "Chromosome X position") +
  theme_ggexon_track(base_size = 10, show_y_axis = TRUE,
                     show_x_grid = FALSE) +
  theme_ggexon_side_strips("left", base_size = 10) +
  theme(axis.title.x = element_text(), axis.title.y = element_text(),
        panel.spacing.y = grid::unit(6, "pt"))
coverage_plot

The panel labels identify the strands, so a separate legend is unnecessary. There is no magnification or secondary-axis transformation. Because the coverage panels have independent y-ranges, equal heights in the two panels need not represent equal signal values; read each panel’s own tick labels.

show_y_axis = TRUE keeps the signal ticks. The annotation y-range closely brackets the gene bodies and their labels below, bringing the models close to the RNASeq tracks. A small panel gap keeps adjacent axis labels readable. coverage_panel_height = 1 / 3 makes each RNASeq panel one-third as tall as the annotation panel, giving the three panels a height ratio of 1:1:3. oob_keep retains boundary intervals for clipping at the genomic window’s edge.

Use scale_panel_coverage("fixed_y") instead if you want all coverage panels to share one signal range, so equal heights represent equal values. This example retains a linear genomic x-axis to align RNASeq and annotation. The Dox tutorial describes the source library, deposited signals, and coverage checks.

7. Place protein mutation labels on genomic gene models

Plot amino-acid substitutions along a protein to see where they fall within protein domains. Lollipop heights show the number of samples carrying each substitution. We first summarize substitutions in protein coordinates, then place their labels on genomic gene models.

Present the input

Protein positions and genomic positions describe different coordinate systems. For this example, create a synthetic mutation summary for a 160-residue protein, plus two synthetic domain intervals. These are teaching data, not biological claims. Counts describe samples carrying each mutation.

raw_mutations <- data.frame(
  gene = "demo-protein",
  event_type = "substitution",
  mutation_hash_or_notation = c("A#18#V", "K#42#R", "G#88#D", "S#140#F"),
  sample_count = c(2L, 5L, 12L, 20L)
)
protein_domains <- data.frame(
  gene_id = "demo-protein", protein_length = 160L,
  start = c(10L, 85L), end = c(60L, 145L),
  Domain = c("Binding", "Catalytic")
)
raw_mutations
#>           gene   event_type mutation_hash_or_notation sample_count
#> 1 demo-protein substitution                    A#18#V            2
#> 2 demo-protein substitution                    K#42#R            5
#> 3 demo-protein substitution                    G#88#D           12
#> 4 demo-protein substitution                   S#140#F           20
protein_domains
#>        gene_id protein_length start end    Domain
#> 1 demo-protein            160    10  60   Binding
#> 2 demo-protein            160    85 145 Catalytic

The mutation reader normalizes gene to gene_id, matching the domain table’s key. protein_length records the full 160-residue protein; the last mutation at residue 140 does not define its end. Protein coordinates here are one-based amino-acid positions.

Construct and inspect the object 

mutation_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".tsv")
domain_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".tsv")
write.table(raw_mutations, mutation_file, sep = "\t", quote = FALSE, row.names = FALSE)
write.table(protein_domains, domain_file, sep = "\t", quote = FALSE, row.names = FALSE)
protein_individual <- add_annotation(
  SynIndividual(id = "synthetic-cohort"),
  SynProteinMutationAnnotation(
    name = "mutation_counts", mutation_file = mutation_file, keytype = "gene_id"
  )
)
protein_individual <- add_annotation(protein_individual, SynProteinDomainAnnotation(
  name = "protein_domains", domain_file = domain_file, keytype = "gene_id"
))
class(protein_individual)
#> [1] "SynIndividual"
#> attr(,"package")
#> [1] "ggexon"
query_protein_mutations(
  protein_individual, annotation = "mutation_counts", genes = "demo-protein"
)[, c("gene_id", "position", "ref", "alt", "mutation", "sample_count")]
#>        gene_id position ref alt mutation sample_count
#> 1 demo-protein       18   A   V     A18V            2
#> 2 demo-protein       42   K   R     K42R            5
#> 3 demo-protein       88   G   D     G88D           12
#> 4 demo-protein      140   S   F    S140F           20

The object owns both annotations. Loading is deferred until inspection or plotting; mutation queries parse hash notation such as A#18#V into a position, reference residue, alternate residue, and label. The query above inspects the input. Neither plotting layer below needs its returned table.

Choose the geom, scales, and theme

At plot build, geom_protein_lollipop() reads mutation_counts, selects demo-protein, matches its domains in protein_domains, and prepares the backbone, stems, and heads. The stored protein length sets the backbone end. Here the target height range equals the input count range, so the identity transform preserves the observed sample counts as head heights.

count_range <- range(raw_mutations$sample_count)
protein_plot <- ggexon(protein_individual) +
  geom_protein_lollipop(
    annotation = "mutation_counts", domain_annotation = "protein_domains",
    genes = "demo-protein",
    mutation_y_by = "sample_count", mutation_y_range = count_range,
    track_ymin = 0.60, track_ymax = 0.68,
    domain_default_ymin = 0.55, domain_default_ymax = 0.75,
    stem_linewidth = 0.9,
    point_colour = "#222222", point_size = 2.5
  ) +
  geom_mutation_label(
    annotation = "mutation_counts", genes = "demo-protein",
    mutation_y_by = "sample_count",
    mutation_y_range = count_range, label_nudge_y = 0,
    angle = 0, vjust = -0.6, size = 3
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Binding = "#0072B2", Catalytic = "#E69F00")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 160, 40), limits = c(0, 160)) +
  scale_y_log10(breaks = c(1, 2, 5, 10, 20), limits = c(0.4, 28)) +
  labs(x = "Amino-acid position", y = "Samples with mutation (log10 scale)",
       fill = "Domain") +
  theme_ggexon_track(base_size = 10, show_y_axis = TRUE, show_legend = TRUE) +
  theme(axis.title = element_text())
protein_plot

The label layer selects the same annotation and gene, and repeats the head-height settings so each label follows its mutation. scale_y_log10() changes the axis spacing while keeping tick labels in sample counts. The backbone and domains sit below count 1 at positive layout coordinates; their vertical positions do not encode counts. A log scale requires positive values. label_nudge_y = 0 anchors labels at their heads, and vjust = -0.6 keeps the text above them. stem_linewidth = 0.9 thickens the grey stems. Keeping show_y_axis = TRUE matters here because y carries a measured quantity. With the default lollipop height range, heights would be rescaled layout positions and should not be labeled as raw counts. No genomic x scale or facet is needed for this single protein-coordinate track.

For transcript- or protein-specific records, set the annotations’ keytype to "transcript_id" or "protein_id" and give both geoms the same ids selector. Select one protein per individual; multiple proteins have separate coordinate systems. A SynSpecies can hold several individuals, selected with species and displayed with facet_genomics(vars(track)).

When a domain table does not contain protein_length, the geom can use one matching sequence stored in protein_seq(), excluding a terminal stop character. Otherwise supply protein_length explicitly. It does not estimate the full length from the last observed mutation.

Project protein features onto the genomic model

A protein residue number is not a chromosome coordinate. Projection follows the transcript’s CDS blocks, so one protein interval can occupy several exons. This example reconnects gene A’s isoforms with a synthetic genome, then places a domain and a mutation on the exon models in genomic base pairs.

Present the raw data

Reuse gtf_file from the first example. Its full transcript contains three CDS blocks; A_skip uses the first and last. Fill a 1,700-base chr1 with unknown bases, then insert complete coding blocks. The first block starts with ATG, the last ends with TAA, and all CDS phases are zero.

coding_blocks <- data.frame(
  start = c(101L, 501L, 901L), end = c(160L, 590L, 960L),
  dna = c(paste0("ATG", strrep("GCC", 19)), strrep("GCC", 30),
          paste0(strrep("GCC", 19), "TAA"))
)
coding_blocks$width <- nchar(coding_blocks$dna)
knitr::kable(coding_blocks[, c("start", "end", "width")])
start end width
101 160 60
501 590 90
901 960 60 
domain_input <- data.frame(
  transcript_id = "A_full", domain = "Domain",
  start = 15L, end = 30L, analysis = "Pfam"
)
mutation_input <- data.frame(
  gene_id = "geneA", transcript_id = "A_full",
  position = 25L, ref = "A", alt = "V",
  sample_count = 4L, mutation = "A25V", source_row_id = 1L
)
knitr::kable(domain_input)
transcript_id domain start end analysis
A_full Domain 15 30 Pfam 
knitr::kable(mutation_input)
gene_id transcript_id position ref alt sample_count mutation source_row_id
geneA A_full 25 A V 4 A25V 1

Domain bounds and mutation positions above are one-based amino-acid coordinates. The mutation table is already normalized; source_row_id records its input row. The mutation belongs to A_full: A25V describes residue 25 of that transcript’s protein, not residue 25 of every isoform.

Construct the sequence and annotation objects

Create a FASTA and a new SynIndividual using the existing GTF. Translation joins each transcript’s CDS in coding order. The output below contains 70 characters for A_full and 40 for A_skip, including a terminal *.

sequence_bases <- rep("N", 1700)
for (i in seq_len(nrow(coding_blocks))) {
  positions <- seq.int(coding_blocks$start[i], coding_blocks$end[i])
  sequence_bases[positions] <- strsplit(coding_blocks$dna[i], "")[[1]]
}
teaching_fasta <- tempfile(fileext = ".fa")
writeLines(c(">chr1", paste0(sequence_bases, collapse = "")), teaching_fasta)
sequence_model <- SynIndividual(
  genome_file = teaching_fasta, annotation_file = gtf_file,
  annotation_format = "gtf", id = "teaching-sequence"
)
sequence_model <- translate_protein(sequence_model, genes = "geneA")
translated <- as.character(protein_seq(sequence_model))
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  transcript = names(translated), residues_including_stop = nchar(translated),
  sequence_start = substr(unname(translated), 1, 12),
  terminal_character = substr(unname(translated), nchar(translated), nchar(translated))
))
transcript residues_including_stop sequence_start terminal_character
A_full A_full 70 MAAAAAAAAAAA *
A_skip A_skip 40 MAAAAAAAAAAA *

Attach both annotations with keytype = "transcript_id", and store the normalized mutation table in memory. This restricts the mutation to its own transcript. The analysis column identifies the domain model; model = "Pfam" selects its records during projection.

teaching_domain_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".tsv")
write.table(domain_input, teaching_domain_file, sep = "\t", quote = FALSE,
            row.names = FALSE)
sequence_model <- add_annotation(sequence_model, SynProteinDomainAnnotation(
  name = "teaching_domains", domain_file = teaching_domain_file,
  keytype = "transcript_id"
))
sequence_model <- add_annotation(sequence_model, SynProteinMutationAnnotation(
  name = "teaching_mutations", mutation_file = "<in-memory>",
  keytype = "transcript_id", mutation_data = mutation_input, lazy = FALSE
))
domain_projection <- project_domains_to_genome(
  sequence_model, annotation = "teaching_domains", model = "Pfam",
  transcripts = "A_full"
)
mutation_projection <- project_mutations_to_genome(
  sequence_model, annotation = "teaching_mutations", genes = "geneA"
)
knitr::kable(domain_projection[, c("transcripts", "xmin", "xmax", "motif")])
transcripts xmin xmax motif
A_full 143 160 Domain
A_full 501 530 Domain 
knitr::kable(mutation_projection[, c("transcripts", "xmin", "xmax", "mutation")])
transcripts xmin xmax mutation
A_full 513 515 A25V

The domain splits into genomic intervals 143-160 and 501-530. A25V maps to 513-515 in A_full and does not appear on A_skip. Using keytype = "gene_id" would instead project the supplied residue number onto every matching isoform. That does not establish an equivalent protein consequence in each isoform; transcript-specific mutations should use a transcript key.

Choose the geoms, scale, and theme

Draw neutral exon models, overlay the projected domain on the A_full row, and add the mutation lollipop to its own transcript. A shared exon_height makes the domain blocks as tall as the exons. Here y_offset = 2 places the single domain row over A_full in this two-isoform layout; inspect row placement when changing transcripts or domain models. The y-axis limits leave balanced space above and below the transcript models and mutation marker. The x-axis includes space before the first exon and beyond the terminal direction triangles, which extend past the last exon.

projection_exon_height <- 0.8
projection_plot <- ggexon(sequence_model) +
  geom_exon(chr = "chr1", subset = c(80, 980), fill = "grey85",
            exon_height = projection_exon_height,
            colour = "grey50", transcript_arrow_length = 25) +
  geom_motif(aes(fill = motif), annotation = "teaching_domains", model = "Pfam",
             chr = "chr1", subset = c(80, 980), y_offset = 2,
             exon_height = projection_exon_height) +
  geom_aa_variant(aes(fill = mutation, label = mutation),
    annotation = "teaching_mutations", genes = "geneA",
    chr = "chr1", subset = c(80, 980), spread = FALSE,
    exon_height = projection_exon_height,
    colour = "grey20", label_angle = 0, label_size = 3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Domain = "#0072B2", A25V = "#D55E00"),
                    name = "Protein feature") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 1500), breaks = c(100, 500, 900, 1300),
                     labels = scales::label_number(big.mark = ","),
                     expand = expansion(mult = 0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0.8, 6.6), expand = expansion(mult = 0)) +
  theme_ggexon_track(base_size = 10, show_legend = TRUE)
projection_plot

This x axis measures genomic base pairs. The preceding protein lollipop example measures amino-acid positions. Projection uses annotation structure; the plotted mutation is supplied teaching data, not a variant inferred from the synthetic FASTA.

8. Aligned DNA and sequence differences

An alignment ribbon summarizes an interval but hides the bases that differ. For a short verified pairwise alignment, alignseq_data() attaches columns to genomic positions and geom_alignseq() draws the sequence detail above gene models. Reuse the annotation behind p_exon2 to keep the gene structure visible while inspecting nucleotide differences.

Present the input

Create two synthetic samples with the same teaching gene models and a short alignment inside gene A’s first exon. The strings below are supplied teaching data, not DNA inferred from the GTF. Each contains six genomic bases, starting at position 131 on chr1. A dash is an alignment gap and consumes no base.

dna <- c(sample_A = "AC-GTAC", sample_B = "ATCG-AC")
anchors <- data.frame(
  sequence = names(dna), start = 131L, strand = "+",
  track = names(dna), chr = "chr1", y = 4.6
)
knitr::kable(data.frame(sequence = names(dna), aligned_DNA = unname(dna)))
sequence aligned_DNA
sample_A AC-GTAC
sample_B ATCG-AC 
knitr::kable(anchors)
sequence start strand track chr y
sample_A 131 + sample_A chr1 4.6
sample_B 131 + sample_B chr1 4.6

Construct and inspect the objects

Attach the same gtf_file used by model and p_exon2 to each sample in a SynSpecies. Each panel will read its gene models from that object. Focus on the gene A window, which contains A_full and A_skip. The anchor’s y = 4.6 places the sequence detail just above the upper transcript model.

dna_models <- SynSpecies(name = "Teaching DNA alignment")
for (sample_id in names(dna)) {
  dna_models <- add_individual(dna_models, SynIndividual(
    id = sample_id, annotation_file = gtf_file, annotation_format = "gtf"
  ))
}
individual_names(dna_models)
#> [1] "sample_A" "sample_B"
dna_columns <- alignseq_data(
  aligned = dna, anchors = anchors, reference = "sample_A",
  details = c(131, 136), flank = 0
)
knitr::kable(dna_columns[, c("track", "column", "base", "position", "event_type")])
track column base position event_type
sample_A 1 A 131 match
sample_A 2 C 132 substitution
sample_A 3 - NA insertion
sample_A 4 G 133 match
sample_A 5 T 134 deletion
sample_A 6 A 135 match
sample_A 7 C 136 match
sample_B 1 A 131 match
sample_B 2 T 132 substitution
sample_B 3 C 133 insertion
sample_B 4 G 134 match
sample_B 5 - NA deletion
sample_B 6 A 135 match
sample_B 7 C 136 match

alignseq_data() returns an inspectable table. It classifies differences relative to sample_A; it does not compute the alignment or infer evolutionary direction. These are two illustrative samples, not sequence differences inferred between the isoforms of one genome.

Choose the geom, scales, and theme

Start with the gene models, then add the alignment as another layer. Keep genomic intron lengths with compress_introns = FALSE. Reuse transcript_colours from p_exon2: blue for A_full and orange for A_skip. Nucleotide colours have their own palette and do not change the transcript fill scale.

dna_gene_plot <- ggexon(dna_models) +
  geom_exon2(
    aes(fill = transcript_id), chr = "chr1", subset = c(80, 980),
    annotation_type = "exon", compress_introns = FALSE,
    exon_height = 0.8, arrow_width = 12, colour = "grey55"
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = transcript_colours, name = "Transcript") +
  facet_genomics(vars(track), ncol = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(80, 980), breaks = c(100, 500, 900)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(1.2, 6.2), expand = expansion(mult = 0)) +
  theme_ggexon_track(base_size = 10, show_x_grid = FALSE, show_legend = TRUE)

The row view suits this seven-column alignment. Sequence letters have equal column spacing within each callout; the gene models retain genomic spacing. Each sequence block has one curved connector from its genomic interval’s displayed midpoint to the centre of the block’s lower edge.

dna_gene_plot +
  geom_alignseq(data = dna_columns, mode = "rows", size = 3.5,
                sequence_position = "center", colour_scheme = "nucleotide")

Use sequence_position = "left", "center", or "right" to choose the sequence block’s horizontal position. The default, "auto", places it near its genomic anchor and moves nearby blocks apart before stacking them. Explicit positions keep blocks aligned and stack overlapping details vertically. Wide blocks are kept inside the panel with room for sequence names. This setting works in both modes and on reversed genomic panels.

Highlight differences instead of nucleotide identity

Set colour_scheme = "difference" to use one colour for mismatches and another for indels, with a neutral colour for the other alignment columns. Here orange marks the mismatch, red marks both insertion and deletion columns, and grey keeps aligned bases in the background. Both samples highlight the same alignment columns, including the gap character.

difference_palette <- c(aligned = "#E6E6E6", mismatch = "#E69F00", indel = "#D73027")
dna_difference_plot <- dna_gene_plot +
  geom_alignseq(
    data = dna_columns, mode = "rows", size = 3.5,
    sequence_position = "center", colour_scheme = "difference",
    difference_colours = difference_palette
  )
dna_difference_plot

Change the three named values in difference_colours to customize this palette. Text switches between black and white to stay readable against the background. With background = FALSE, only the mismatch and indel letters receive highlight colours. Ambiguous IUPAC bases remain neutral and are not classified as verified mismatches.

For larger regions, mode = "markers" draws differences and uses details only for selected callouts. Match track names to existing annotation panels when adding DNA detail to a comparison. The AS3MT example uses this approach at a real locus.

9. Equal gene slots for a presence and order comparison

Base-pair spacing can obscure corresponding gene families across loci. A shared slot template makes occupied and empty positions visible, changing the meaning of the x axis to comparison slots.

Present the input

These synthetic clusters have genes assigned to three slots. Cluster B has no row for slot 2; this input omission alone does not establish gene loss.

slot_input <- data.frame(
  cluster = c("A", "A", "A", "B", "B"),
  position = c(100, 300, 1000, 500, 900),
  slot = c("s1", "s2", "s3", "s1", "s3"),
  strand = c("+", "-", "+", "-", "+")
)
knitr::kable(slot_input)
cluster position slot strand
A 100 s1 +
A 300 s2 -
A 1000 s3 +
B 500 s1 -
B 900 s3 +

Prepare the plotting data

Retain genomic positions in x. The strip scale maps these to the explicit template rather than requiring us to overwrite source coordinates.

slot_data <- transform(slot_input, x = position, y = 1, track = cluster,
                       gene_key = slot, genomic_x = position)
slot_order <- c("s1", "s2", "s3")

Choose the geom, scales, facet, and theme

geom_genebox() uses equal-size squares with strand arrows. strip_scale_x() reserves every slot, including unoccupied ones. scale_x_facet_labels() names each facet’s slots, and coord_fixed() keeps boxes square. The clean theme retains ordinary axis labels.

ggexon(slot_data) +
  geom_genebox(data = slot_data, aes(fill = slot), box_size = 0.65) +
  facet_grid(. ~ cluster) +
  strip_scale_x(slot_order = slot_order, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_facet_labels(
    cluster, labels = list(A = c("A1", "A2", "A3"), B = c("B1", "B2", "B3"))
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(s1 = "#0072B2", s2 = "#D55E00", s3 = "#009E73")) +
  coord_fixed(ratio = 1) +
  theme_ggexon_clean(base_size = 10) +
  theme(axis.title = element_blank(), axis.text.y = element_blank(),
        panel.grid = element_blank(), legend.position = "none")

The x axis now names supplied slots, not base pairs. With Syn-backed data, geom_genebox(anchor = "start"), "middle", or "end" chooses the coding anchor before scaling.

10. Align genomic tracks to a tree

A phylogenetic ordering can make a multi-genome comparison easier to read. ggexon aligns one spanning rectangular tree to genomic rows without manual positioning of separate plots.

Present the input

Create two small synthetic gene tracks and supply a synthetic Newick tree. The intervals and branch lengths are illustrative. This optional example requires ape and ggtree.

genes <- data.frame(
  track = rep(c("reference", "query"), each = 2),
  xmin = c(100, 400, 1100, 1600), xmax = c(250, 600, 1300, 1750),
  y = 1, strand = c("+", "-", "+", "-"), gene = rep(c("A", "B"), 2)
)
tree_text <- "(reference:0.1,query:0.2);"
tree_text
#> [1] "(reference:0.1,query:0.2);"
knitr::kable(genes)
track xmin xmax y strand gene
reference 100 250 1 + A
reference 400 600 1 - B
query 1100 1300 1 + A
query 1600 1750 1 - B

Prepare the objects

Tree-tip names must match track IDs, or be mapped with the individual argument to geom_genomic_tree().

tree_available <- requireNamespace("ape", quietly = TRUE) &&
  requireNamespace("ggtree", quietly = TRUE)
if (tree_available) {
  teaching_tree <- ape::read.tree(text = tree_text)
  tree_tracks <- transform(genes, track = as.character(track))
}

Choose the geom, scales, facet, and theme

geom_genomic_tree() attaches the tree; facet_genomictree() orders and aligns the panels. Genomic x ranges and tree branch lengths have separate scales and meanings. This compact view hides the branch-length ruler; branch lengths remain specified in the Newick input.

if (tree_available) {
  ggexon(tree_tracks) +
    geom_genetag(aes(fill = gene), show_label = FALSE) +
    geom_genomic_tree(tree = teaching_tree, tree_width = grid::unit(1.2, "in")) +
    facet_genomictree(scales = "free_x", show_tree_x_axis = FALSE) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c(A = "#0072B2", B = "#D55E00")) +
    scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_number()) +
    theme_ggexon_genomictree(base_size = 10)
} else {
  cat("Install ape and ggtree to render this optional example.")
}

For repeated multi-locus comparisons, store comparable windows in a SynLocusSet, attach it with add_locus_set(), and use use_locus_grid(). This records the chosen loci alongside the individuals.

11. Correct an annotation and compare the result

A gene-model correction is easier to review when it remains attached to the annotation and you can still plot the original. A patch records the target, replacement features, and a name for the change.

Present the correction

Shorten gene A’s middle exon from 590 to 560 in this synthetic exercise. Supply the complete corrected gene model, including its unchanged children.

corrected_ranges <- query_features(model, genes = "geneA", feature_type = NULL, all = TRUE)
change <- as.character(S4Vectors::mcols(corrected_ranges)$type) %in% c("exon", "CDS") &
  BiocGenerics::start(corrected_ranges) == 501
BiocGenerics::end(corrected_ranges)[change] <- 560L
knitr::kable(as.data.frame(corrected_ranges)[,
  c("start", "end", "type", "gene_id", "transcript_id")])
start end type gene_id transcript_id
101 960 gene geneA NA
101 960 transcript geneA A_full
101 160 exon geneA A_full
501 560 exon geneA A_full
901 960 exon geneA A_full
101 160 CDS geneA A_full
501 560 CDS geneA A_full
901 960 CDS geneA A_full
101 960 transcript geneA A_skip
101 160 exon geneA A_skip
901 960 exon geneA A_skip
101 160 CDS geneA A_skip
901 960 CDS geneA A_skip

Construct and apply the patch 

correction <- SynAnnotationPatch(
  name = "shorter-middle-exon", target_ids = "geneA", mode = "replace",
  patch_data = corrected_ranges
)
corrected_model <- patch_annotation(model, correction)
names(list_patches(corrected_model))
#> [1] "shorter-middle-exon"

patch_annotation_from_gff() imports corrections from a small GFF. Replacing models clears stale sequence caches; recompute derived sequences afterwards.

reset_patches() clears all recorded patches and restores the base feature annotation. A removal is also recorded as a patch, so it can be inspected and reset in the same way. These operations return updated objects; model remains available for the comparison below.

restored_model <- reset_patches(corrected_model)
length(list_patches(restored_model))
#> [1] 0

without_gene_b <- patch_annotation(
  model, patch = NULL, target_ids = "geneB", mode = "remove",
  name = "remove-gene-b"
)
names(list_patches(without_gene_b))
#> [1] "remove-gene-b"
unique(as.character(S4Vectors::mcols(annotation_data(without_gene_b))$gene_id))
#> [1] "geneA"

Choose the geom, scales, facet, and theme

Retain the same base-pair scale before and after to compare the boundary. Use uncompressed geom_exon2() models so the direction arrows sit at the terminal exons in this compact comparison.

before <- load_annotation(SynIndividual(
  annotation_file = gtf_file, annotation_format = "gtf", id = "before"
))
after <- load_annotation(SynIndividual(
  annotation_file = gtf_file, annotation_format = "gtf", id = "after"
))
after <- patch_annotation(after, correction)
curation <- add_individual(SynSpecies("Annotation curation"), before)
curation <- add_individual(curation, after)
ggexon(curation) +
  geom_exon2(aes(fill = transcript_id), chr = "chr1", subset = c(80, 980),
             compress_introns = FALSE, arrow_width = 12) +
  facet_genomics(vars(track), ncol = 1, scales = "fixed", strip.position = "left") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = transcript_colours) +
  scale_panel_annotation("fixed_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(100, 500, 900)) +
  theme_ggexon_track(base_size = 10) +
  theme_ggexon_side_strips("left", base_size = 10)

12. Query a VCF layer and mark variant positions

A VCF records allele changes at genomic positions. The feature annotation and variant layer remain separate: attaching a VCF does not change the gene model. This short example reuses model from the first example.

Present the input

Create three synthetic single-nucleotide variants on the same chr1 as the teaching GTF. VCF POS uses one-based coordinates; these example alleles are teaching labels and have not been checked against a reference FASTA.

vcf_lines <- c(
  "##fileformat=VCFv4.2",
  "#CHROM\tPOS\tID\tREF\tALT\tQUAL\tFILTER\tINFO",
  "chr1\t125\tv1\tA\tG\t60\tPASS\t.",
  "chr1\t535\tv2\tC\tT\t80\tPASS\t.",
  "chr1\t925\tv3\tG\tA\t50\tPASS\t."
)
cat(vcf_lines, sep = "\n")
#> ##fileformat=VCFv4.2
#> #CHROM   POS ID  REF ALT QUAL    FILTER  INFO
#> chr1 125 v1  A   G   60  PASS    .
#> chr1 535 v2  C   T   80  PASS    .
#> chr1 925 v3  G   A   50  PASS    .
vcf_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".vcf")
writeLines(vcf_lines, vcf_file)

Construct and inspect the object

Attach a named SynVCFAnnotation, retrieve it, and query the displayed interval. Plain-text VCF is sufficient for this small example. Large BGZF VCFs can use a tabix index for regional access. BCF parsing is unavailable.

variant_model <- add_annotation(
  model, SynVCFAnnotation(name = "variants", vcf_file = vcf_file)
)
variant_rows <- as.data.frame(query_variants(
  get_annotation(variant_model, "variants"),
  chr = "chr1", start = 80, end = 980
))
knitr::kable(variant_rows[, c("CHROM", "POS", "ID", "REF", "ALT")])
CHROM POS ID REF ALT
chr1 125 v1 A G
chr1 535 v2 C T
chr1 925 v3 G A 
variant_rows$allele <- paste0(variant_rows$REF, ">", variant_rows$ALT)

Choose the geoms, scales, and theme

Use the stored feature annotation for exon models and an ordinary geom_vline() for the queried variant positions. Both use the same genomic x coordinates. The lines mark sites across transcript rows; they do not represent frequencies, coverage, or allele-specific transcript structures.

vcf_plot <- ggexon(variant_model) +
  geom_exon(chr = "chr1", subset = c(80, 980), fill = "grey65",
            transcript_arrow_length = 25) +
  geom_vline(
    data = variant_rows, aes(xintercept = POS, colour = allele),
    linewidth = 0.6, linetype = "dashed", inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("A>G" = "#0072B2", "C>T" = "#D55E00", "G>A" = "#009E73"),
                      name = "REF > ALT") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(100, 500, 900), labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  theme_ggexon_track(base_size = 10, show_legend = TRUE)
vcf_plot

Choose a view for your question

Question Object or preparation Geometry Scale and theme
Which exons and isoforms are annotated? SynIndividual + features geom_exon() Genomic bp; track theme
How do exon structures compare across long introns? Feature layer geom_exon2() scale_x_ggexon_genomic(); piecewise guide
What is the order and direction of genes? Feature layer + plot labels geom_genetag(), geom_genelabel() Genomic bp or strip scale; track theme
Which intervals align between genomes? SynSpecies + SynPairAlignment geom_nuclink() Independent genomic x; pairwise theme
How do gene spans relate to aligned blocks? SynSpecies + stored alignment and panel windows geom_genetag(), geom_synteny_link() Independent genomic x; pairwise theme
How does signal vary across a locus? SynBigWigAnnotation geom_coverage() Genomic x; explicit coverage y policy
Where are protein domains and mutations? Mutation and domain tables/layers geom_protein_lollipop(), geom_motif(), geom_aa_variant() Protein residues or projected genomic bp
Where are genomic variants recorded? SynVCFAnnotation + query_variants() Exons + ordinary geom_vline() Genomic bp; track theme
Which bases differ in an existing alignment? alignseq_data() geom_alignseq() Anchored genomic coordinates; track theme
Which comparison slots are occupied? Gene-slot table geom_genebox() strip_scale_x(), facet labels; clean theme
How do loci relate to a supplied tree? Matching tracks and tree geom_genomic_tree() facet_genomictree(); genomic-tree theme

theme_ggexon_base() is the common background-free foundation; theme_ggexon_clean() keeps ordinary axes and grids. Choose the track theme when y only positions annotations; retain a numeric y axis for quantitative summaries. Side-strip styling supplements a theme and must match the facet’s strip.position. Add ordinary theme() overrides after the complete theme.

Export a saved plot object with explicit dimensions and inspect the result. For example, ggsave("exon-models.pdf", plot = p_exons, width = 9, height = 3.5) exports the first model view.

The function reference describes individual classes, geoms, facets, and scales. The four biological tutorials expand these recipes with documented sources.
